title: The Adventures of Pinocchio
author: Carlo Collodi
short_summary: A poor woodcarver called Geppetto carves a puppet out of a strange piece of talking wood and names him Pinocchio. The puppet runs off before he is even finished, and the book that follows is a long chain of bad decisions: a squashed cricket, two burned-off feet, a swindle in the Field of Wonders, five months in the Land of Toys, a pair of donkey's ears — and, at the very bottom of it, the inside of a shark.
extended_summary:
The log Geppetto is given can already talk. He carves it into a puppet, and Pinocchio runs out of the door before the paint is dry. When a Talking Cricket who has lived in the house for years tells him that boys who will not work come to a bad end, Pinocchio throws a hammer at it and kills it. That night he falls asleep with his feet on the brazier and wakes to find them burned off, and Geppetto carves him new ones and sells his own coat to buy him a schoolbook.

Pinocchio sells the book for a ticket to a puppet show. The showman, Fire Eater, gives him five gold pieces for Geppetto, and on the way home a Fox and a Cat persuade him that if he buries the coins in the Field of Wonders a money tree will grow. They rob him, hang him from an oak, and he is rescued by a girl with blue hair. When she asks what became of the coins, he lies, and his nose grows with every lie.

Later he runs off with a friend to the Land of Toys, where there is no school and every day is a holiday, and after five months the boys there grow long ears and begin to bray: they have all turned into donkeys. Sold, lamed and thrown into the sea, Pinocchio becomes a puppet again and is swallowed by the Terrible Shark — where he finds Geppetto, who has been inside it for two years. They escape, and Pinocchio, working to keep the old man and the sick Fairy, finally wakes up one morning as a real boy.

questions.prompt: A Talking Cricket warns Pinocchio that boys who refuse to work come to a bad end. What does Pinocchio do?

options: Throws a hammer at it and kills it
Promises to obey it and goes to school
Puts it outside and shuts the window
Takes it with him as a travelling companion

questions.explanation: This is chapter four, and it is the moment that tells you what kind of book this is. The film version turns the cricket into a friendly guide; Collodi's puppet kills it on the spot — and then spends the rest of the book being haunted by it.

questions.prompt: Pinocchio falls asleep with his feet resting on the brazier. What has happened by morning?

options: His feet have burned completely away
The brazier has set fire to Geppetto's bench
His legs have grown twice as long as before
The paint on his feet has blistered and peeled

questions.explanation: He is made of wood, and Collodi never lets the reader forget it. Geppetto carves him a new pair without complaining — and then sells his only coat to buy the schoolbook, which Pinocchio sells the same morning.

questions.prompt: To buy Pinocchio a schoolbook, Geppetto goes out into the cold and sells his own ___.
questions.explanation: It is the second time in two chapters that Geppetto gives up something he needs. The book keeps a very careful account of what the old man loses and what the puppet costs him, which is why the ending has to be earned rather than granted.

questions.prompt: The Fox and the Cat tell Pinocchio what to do with his five gold pieces. What do they persuade him to do?

options: Bury them in a field so a money tree will grow
Buy a share in a puppet theatre of his own
Hide them inside a hollow tree until morning
Exchange them for a map to a hidden treasure

questions.explanation: Bury the coins in the Field of Wonders, water them, and a tree hung with gold will come up by morning. Pinocchio believes it because he wants it to be true — and the two of them come back in disguise the same night to dig the money up.

questions.prompt: Put Pinocchio's first misadventures in the order they happen.

items: Geppetto carves a puppet out of a talking piece of wood
Pinocchio throws a hammer at the Talking Cricket
He falls asleep and his feet are burned away
He sells his schoolbook to see a puppet show
Fire Eater gives him five gold pieces for Geppetto
The Fox and the Cat take him to the Field of Wonders

questions.explanation: Six disasters, and the book is barely a third over. Collodi's structure is relentless: every time Pinocchio is given something — feet, a book, five gold coins — he loses it within a chapter, and always by his own choice.

questions.prompt: Match each character to their part in Pinocchio's story.

right: Carves him, and sells his coat for a schoolbook
Gives good advice and is killed for it
The puppet showman who hands over five coins
Cuts him down from the oak and asks about the money

questions.explanation: Notice that the two people who help Pinocchio most are the ones he treats worst. Collodi is not writing about a naughty boy who needs encouragement; he is writing about one who has to learn what other people have already spent on him.

questions.prompt: The Land of Toys is not what it is advertised to be. Sort each item.

options.label: Every single day is a holiday
Games and fun from morning to night
Their ears grow long and furry
They lose their voices and start to bray
They are sold off to work as animals

questions.explanation: The left-hand column is a real advertisement and the right-hand column is the real price, and five months pass between them. It is the most frightening sequence in the book precisely because nothing is forced on anybody: every boy there chose to come.

questions.prompt: What becomes of the boys who stay in the Land of Toys?

options: They slowly turn into donkeys
They forget their own names and families
They are locked up and made to work at night
They grow older by a year with every month

questions.explanation: Ears first, then the braying, then four legs — and then they are sold. Collodi's punishment is a literal one: boys who behave like animals become animals, and the book follows Pinocchio all the way through being bought, lamed and thrown into the sea.

questions.prompt: In chapter four Pinocchio kills the Talking Cricket, who had done nothing but give him good advice. He is never punished for it by anyone. Should the book have punished him? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'should have been punished' answer notices that this is the worst thing anyone does in the book and that it is passed over in a page. A strong 'no' answer notices that everything that happens to Pinocchio afterwards is the consequence of ignoring exactly that advice, and that the Cricket comes back to say so. Accept either, argued from the book.

questions.prompt: Pinocchio is ruined every time by an offer that sounds wonderful: a money tree, a country with no school. Invent one more offer that would tempt him. Who makes it, what do they promise, and what would the real price turn out to be?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong invention has all three parts and, crucially, a price that fits the promise the way donkeys' ears fit a country with no school. An offer with an unrelated punishment attached has missed how Collodi's traps work.

questions.prompt: Pinocchio finds Geppetto again inside a huge sea creature — not a whale, as people often say, but an enormous ___.
questions.explanation: Collodi's monster is a shark — the Terrible Shark, five storeys high — and Geppetto has been living inside it for two years on the stores of a ship it swallowed. The whale belongs to the film, not the book.

questions.prompt: What finally turns Pinocchio into a real boy?

options: Working to support Geppetto and the sick Fairy
Surviving his escape from inside the shark
Telling the truth about the five gold pieces
Refusing to go back to the Land of Toys

questions.explanation: Not a brave deed and not a wish granted: months of ordinary work — turning a water wheel, weaving baskets, giving away what he has saved. Collodi makes the transformation the last thing in the book because it has to be paid for, and it takes as long as it takes.
